kurals.tamil:
உட்கப் படாஅர் ஒளியிழப்பர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகு வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Utkap pataaar oliyizhappar enjnjaandrum
katkaadhal kondozhugu vaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who live with a constant craving for liquor are never held in awe by their enemies, and they lose the lustre of the good name they once had.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a strong, respected team captain who starts doing something silly every day. Soon nobody on the other team worries about him any more, and even his own friends stop looking up to him. The Kural says a love of strong drink does exactly that: it makes a person look small.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with two losses: the drinker is not utkappadaar (உட்கப்படாஅர், 'not feared', from உட்கு, awe or dread, with an alapedai lengthening) and he oliyizhappar (ஒளியிழப்பர், 'loses his lustre'), where oli (ஒளி) means both brightness and reputation. The habitual sense comes from katkaadhal kondozhuguvaar (கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகுவார்), 'those who conduct themselves holding a love of toddy', so the target is addiction rather than a single lapse. Because the chapter sits in Porutpaal beside Varaivin Magalir (92) and Soothu (94), the traditional reading inherited from Parimelazhagar treats it as one of the vices a ruler must shun; Puliyur Kesikan's gloss on thirukkural.net explicitly makes the subject 'kings' whose enemies no longer fear them and who lose the fame won by their ancestors. Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the subject general. The couplet is identical on ytamizh and thirukkural.net, though the two sites attach the Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar glosses in opposite order.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Son killed sire, and sire killed son, O Bharata. Inebriated with wine, they rushed and fell upon one another.”
hinduism.explanation: At Prabhasa the invincible Vrishni and Andhaka heroes begin a drinking revel, quarrel, and destroy their own clan before Krishna's eyes.
hinduism.tie_back: A warrior people who were once feared lose all their glory through drink, as the Kural warns.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, Section 3 (K. M. Ganguli trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the epic also attributes the ruin to a curse, so drink is a main cause but not the only one.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them! … but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.”
christianity.explanation: Isaiah condemns the leaders of Judah who spend their days drinking and lose sight of what truly matters.
christianity.tie_back: The prophet's ‘woe’ on habitual drinkers matches the Kural's picture of a person whose constant craving ruins his standing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same habitual-drinking target, but Isaiah stresses spiritual blindness rather than loss of awe and fame.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allāh], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ties avoiding intoxicants directly to falah, true success and flourishing.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's drinker loses his lustre; the Qur'an promises success to those who abstain.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (including the source's spelling 'alters'); the link is general prosperity rather than the specific loss of awe.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wine is not for kings, O Lemuel; Not for kings to drink, Nor any strong drink for princes, Lest they drink and forget what has been ordained, And infringe on the rights of the poor.”
judaism.explanation: The queen mother of King Lemuel warns that rulers who drink forget the law and fail in justice.
judaism.tie_back: Like the traditional royal reading of this Kural, Proverbs says drink is unworthy of a ruler and destroys his authority.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match to the king-centred reading; the focus is justice more than prestige.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who plays with dice and drinks intoxicants, goes to women who are dear unto others as their own lives, associates with the mean and not with elders — he declines just as the moon during the waning half.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the young householder Sigala that drink is among the habits that make a man's fortunes wane.
buddhism.tie_back: The waning moon is a direct image of the Kural's oliyizhappar, the drinker who loses his light.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the loss-of-lustre image matches closely, though drink is one item in a list.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The man-eating Cyclops Polyphemus, terror of Odysseus' crew, accepts strong wine, drinks himself into a stupor and is blinded by the very men he had trapped.
greek_mythology.explanation: A monster everyone feared becomes helpless as soon as wine takes hold of him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Wine strips Polyphemus of the dread he inspired, as the Kural says the drinker is no longer feared.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear story parallel, but Polyphemus is tricked into one bout rather than shown as a habitual drinker.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “This evil has betrayed to their enemies the most spirited and warlike races; … this evil has conquered by the wine-cup those who in the field were invincible.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca lists the military disasters drunkenness has brought on peoples and leaders, Alexander among them.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's point is the Kural's: the drinker stops being a threat to his enemies.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 83.22 (Gummere trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified on Wikisource; very close to the 'not feared by foes' half of the couplet.

kurals.tamil:
உண்ணற்க கள்ளை உணில்உண்க சான்றோரான்
எண்ணப் படவேண்டா தார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Unnarka kallai unilunka saandroraan
ennap padavendaa thaar.
kurals.meaning: Do not drink liquor. If anyone must drink, let it be only those who do not care to be thought well of by good and wise people.
kurals.elementary: Suppose a teacher says, ‘Don't cheat on the test. Well, if you really want to cheat, go ahead, but only if you don't care whether anyone ever trusts you again.’ The teacher isn't giving permission. She is showing how much it costs. The Kural speaks about drinking the same way.
kurals.university: The first clause is a flat prohibition, unnarka kallai (உண்ணற்க கள்ளை, 'drink not toddy'). The second, unil unka (உணில் உண்க, 'if you would drink, drink'), is an ironic concession, a figure the commentators call igazhchchi (இகழ்ச்சி, scorn). It limits the 'permission' to those who are saandroraan ennappada vendaathaar (சான்றோரான் எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்), people who do not wish to be esteemed by the saandror (சான்றோர், the noble and learned). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all keep this ironic reading. Puliyur Kesikan adds that the first clause is addressed to arivudaiyor (the wise), since toddy clouds the mind. The structure foreshadows Kural 923, where the saandror again sit in judgment. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The wretched Brahmana who from this day, unable to resist the temptation, will drink wine shall be regarded as having lost his virtue, shall be reckoned to have committed the sin of slaying a Brahmana, shall be hated both in this and the other worlds.”
hinduism.explanation: After unknowingly drinking his disciple Kacha's ashes mixed in his wine, the sage Shukra bans drink for Brahmanas.
hinduism.tie_back: Shukra's decree states the Kural's price outright: whoever drinks gives up the esteem of the virtuous.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 76 (K. M. Ganguli trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it is a caste-specific rule, but the loss-of-esteem logic matches.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to refuse drunkenness and seek a better kind of fullness.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's opening clause, it is a direct command not to give oneself to drink.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the prohibition, but not the ironic concession about esteem.

islam.quote_or_event: “If a large amount of anything causes intoxication, a small amount of it is prohibited.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet closes the loophole of drinking ‘only a little’.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's mock permission and this hadith both refuse any respectable middle ground for drinking.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on sunnah.com; same uncompromising stance, different rhetorical form.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Drink no wine or other intoxicant, you or your sons, when you enter the Tent of Meeting, that you may not die. This is a law for all time throughout the ages, for you must distinguish between the sacred and the profane, and between the impure and the pure;”
judaism.explanation: Priests must be sober to keep the clear judgment their sacred role requires.
judaism.tie_back: Those who hope to be counted among the worthy must abstain, which is the Kural's implied ideal.
judaism._accuracy_note: Limited to priests on duty in the sanctuary; a partial parallel only.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who destroys life, utters lies, takes what is not given, goes to another man's wife, and is addicted to intoxicating drinks — such a man digs up his own root even in this world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada puts addiction to drink alongside the gravest moral failings.
buddhism.tie_back: Choosing drink means choosing to stand outside the company of the good, just as the Kural implies.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong condemnation, though it does not mention the esteem of the wise.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Scythian sage Anacharsis is reported to have said that the vine bears three clusters: the first of pleasure, the second of drunkenness, the third of disgust.
greek_mythology.explanation: Anacharsis traces how drinking moves from pleasure to drunkenness to disgust.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, he points to where drinking ends: in the contempt of others.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 1.103 (Hicks trans.)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory and not re-verified this session; Greek wisdom tradition rather than myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato's Socrates says the guardians of the ideal city must avoid drunkenness above all, since a guardian is the last person who should be drunk and not know where he is.
philosophy.explanation: Those trusted with the city must keep sober judgment.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato, like the Kural, makes sobriety the condition for being counted among the worthy.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not verified verbatim; the Stephanus location is approximate.

kurals.tamil:
ஈன்றாள் முகத்தேயும் இன்னாதால் என்மற்றுச்
சான்றோர் முகத்துக் களி.
kurals.transliteration:
Eendraal mugaththeyum innaadhaal enmatruch
chaandror mugaththuk kali.
kurals.meaning: Drunkenness is painful to see even for the mother who bore a person, who forgives almost anything. How much worse must it look to the wise, who tolerate no fault?
kurals.elementary: Your mom loves you no matter what, even after you spill juice on the carpet. But some behaviour makes even a loving mom sad and embarrassed. If something upsets the person who forgives you most, imagine how it looks to a strict teacher or a respected elder.
kurals.university: The couplet argues from the lesser to the greater. Eendraal (ஈன்றாள், 'she who bore') is the most forgiving witness a person has; Puliyur Kesikan glosses her as the one who rejoices whatever her child does. Even 'in her face' (mugaththeyum, முகத்தேயும்) kali (களி, intoxication) is innaadhu (இன்னாது, painful). The question en matru (என் மற்று, 'what, then?') carries the argument to the saandror (சான்றோர்), whom Mu. Varadarasanar describes as having the nature of rebuking faults (குற்றம் கடியும் இயல்பு). The repeated mugam (முகம், face) presents shame as something seen. Kalaignar reads the subject as the son his mother cannot bear to look at. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Chandogya Upanishad names the one who drinks liquor among four great sinners who ‘fall’, along with the thief of gold, the violator of the teacher's bed and the slayer of a Brahmin, and adds as a fifth whoever keeps company with them.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad treats drinking as a fall so grave that it stains even those around the drinker.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, drink brings grief and disgrace not only to the drinker but to those near him.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim this session; it fits the gravity of the vice but has no mother image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father, and told his two brethren without. And Shem and Japheth took a garment, … and covered the nakedness of their father; and their faces were backward, and they saw not their father's nakedness.”
christianity.explanation: After Noah gets drunk, his own sons cannot bear to look at him and cover his shame.
christianity.tie_back: As with the mother in the Kural, it is the closest family who find the drunkard painful to see.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified; the family members here are sons, not the mother, and the lesser-to-greater argument is missing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Hamza was drunk and his eyes were red. … and then said, ‘You are not but my father's slaves.’ When the Prophet (ﷺ) understood that Hamza was drunk, he retreated, walking backwards went out and we left with him.”
islam.explanation: Before Islam forbade wine, the Prophet's own uncle Hamza, drunk, insults the Prophet, who quietly withdraws.
islam.tie_back: Drunkenness in the presence of the most honoured person turns into a painful scene of dishonour, as the Kural says.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on sunnah.com; strong 'before the noble' parallel, and a kinsman is involved.

judaism.quote_or_event: “his father and mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his town at the public place of his community. They shall say to the elders of his town, ‘This son of ours is disloyal and defiant; he does not heed us. He is a glutton and a drunkard.’”
judaism.explanation: The law of the wayward son has the parents themselves bring their drunkard son before the town's elders.
judaism.tie_back: The pain begins with the mother and father and ends before the elders, the same movement as the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified; a legal case rather than a moral maxim, but it pairs parents and elders exactly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In five ways, young householder, the parents thus ministered to as the East by their children, show their compassion: (i) they restrain them from evil, (ii) they encourage them to do good, …”
buddhism.explanation: In the Sigalovada the parents' love shows itself in holding their children back from wrong, intoxicants included, which the same sutta lists as a ruinous habit.
buddhism.tie_back: A parent's grief at a child's drinking comes from this protective love, which the Kural appeals to.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified wording, but the link to drinking comes from elsewhere in the sutta; a weak match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides' Alcestis, Heracles drinks and sings in King Admetus' house without knowing it is in mourning; a household servant is appalled, and Heracles is ashamed once he learns the truth.
greek_mythology.explanation: The revelry of a hero who is loved and honoured becomes painful to the house that welcomed him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Even friends and household are hurt by the sight of someone in drink, as the Kural says of a mother.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Plot summary from memory; Heracles' drinking comes from ignorance rather than vice, so the parallel is loose.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Show how base it is to pour down more liquor than one can carry, and not to know the capacity of one's own stomach; show how often the drunkard does things which make him blush when he is sober; state that drunkenness is nothing but a condition of insanity purposely assumed.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca sets aside Zeno's clever syllogisms against drink and says the honest case against drunkenness is simply to show how shameful it is. He adds that it strips away the sense of shame that otherwise holds men back from wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Seneca makes the drunkard's shame, seen through the eyes of others and of his own sober self, the main charge against drink.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 83.18-19 (tr. Richard Mott Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Gummere, Letter 83 'On Drunkenness', §18; a footnote marker removed). Strong thematic match on the disgrace of drunkenness, but Seneca does not use the Kural's contrast between the forgiving mother and the stricter wise.

kurals.tamil:
நாண்என்னும் நல்லாள் புறங்கொடுக்கும் கள்ளென்னும்
பேணாப் பெருங்குற்றத் தார்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Naanennum nallaal purangodukkum kallennum
penaap perungutrath thaarkku.
kurals.meaning: The noble lady called Modesty turns her back and leaves those who commit the great and hateful fault called drink.
kurals.elementary: Picture Modesty as a kind lady who walks beside you and whispers ‘don't do that, it's embarrassing.’ The Kural says that when someone gets drunk she turns around and walks away, so there's no one left to stop him doing shameful things.
kurals.university: Naan (நாண், modesty, the sense of shame) is personified as a nallaal (நல்லாள், a good woman). Purangodukkum (புறங்கொடுக்கும்), literally 'gives the back', is a battlefield term for retreat, so Modesty flees from the drinker as a beaten warrior flees. The parallel compounds naanennum nallaal / kallennum penaap perungutram (கள்ளென்னும் பேணாப் பெருங்குற்றம், 'the great fault called toddy, which none would cherish') set a personified virtue against a personified vice. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses that she will not stand before the drinker; Solomon Pappaiah renders it as Modesty showing her back and going away. The idea looks ahead to Naanudaimai (chapter 102). The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Manusmriti counts drinking sura among the mahapatakas, the great sins, together with killing a Brahmin, stealing gold and violating the teacher's bed, and prescribes severe penances for it.
hinduism.explanation: Dharma law ranks drinking among the gravest offences a twice-born person can commit.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's perungutram, ‘great fault’, has a formal counterpart in Manu's ‘great sin’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased without a verse number; it matches 'great fault' but not the personified Modesty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.”
christianity.explanation: Paul sets decent, honest conduct against drunkenness and the shameless behaviour that comes with it.
christianity.tie_back: In both texts drunkenness is where decency and modesty give way.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified; 'honestly' here means decently, which is close to the Kural's naan.

islam.quote_or_event: “An adulterer, at the time he is committing illegal sexual intercourse is not a believer; and a person, at the time of drinking an alcoholic drink is not a believer; …”
islam.explanation: At the moment of drinking, faith is said to leave the drinker.
islam.tie_back: As the Kural's Modesty turns her back, faith (which other hadith pair with modesty) steps away from the drinker.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified; the hadith speaks of faith, not modesty itself, so the match is structural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You shall be sated with shame Rather than glory: Drink in your turn and stagger! The cup in GOD's right hand Shall come around to you, And disgrace to your glory.”
judaism.explanation: Habakkuk pronounces that the one who makes others drunk will himself drink and stagger into disgrace.
judaism.tie_back: Drink brings disgrace in place of dignity, the same exchange the Kural describes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified; prophetic judgment imagery rather than ethical advice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are, young householder, these six evil consequences in indulging in intoxicants which cause infatuation and heedlessness: (i) loss of wealth, (ii) increase of quarrels, (iii) susceptibility to disease, (iv) earning an evil reputation, (v) shameless exposure of body, (vi) weakening of intellect.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists shamelessness among the direct results of intoxicants.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Shameless exposure’ is the Buddhist way of saying Modesty has left the drinker.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it directly names loss of shame as a consequence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “When the wine had got into his head he went mad and did ill deeds about the house of Peirithous; this angered the heroes who were there assembled, …”
greek_mythology.explanation: The centaur Eurytion, drunk at a wedding feast, behaves disgracefully in his host's house and is punished.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Once wine took hold, all restraint and sense of shame left Eurytion, as the Kural says.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a story of shameless conduct with no personified Modesty.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Drunkenness kindles and discloses every kind of vice, and removes the sense of shame that veils our evil undertakings. For more men abstain from forbidden actions because they are ashamed of sinning than because their inclinations are good.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca says drink takes away the shame that usually keeps people from wrongdoing.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's picture of Modesty leaving the drinker.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 83.19 (Gummere trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified on Wikisource; a near one-to-one match.

kurals.tamil:
கையறி யாமை உடைத்தே பொருள்கொடுத்து
மெய்யறி யாமை கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaiyari yaamai udaiththe porulkoduththu
meyyari yaamai kolal.
kurals.meaning: To pay good money in order to buy a state where you no longer know yourself shows a person who does not understand what he is doing.
kurals.elementary: Imagine spending all your pocket money on a ticket for a ride that makes you so dizzy you can't remember your own name, and then trips you over. You'd be paying to lose yourself. The Kural says buying liquor is that kind of bad deal.
kurals.university: The couplet balances two forms of ignorance: kaiyariyaamai (கையறியாமை) and meyyariyaamai (மெய்யறியாமை). The second clearly means not knowing one's own body or self, the stupor that porul koduththu (பொருள்கொடுத்து, 'by giving wealth') one kolal (கொளல், 'takes on'). The first is read in two ways. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as not knowing what to do, a failure of practical sense. Puliyur Kesikan (thirukkural.net) reads it as having one's past karma as its cause, so only an ill-fated person would make such a bargain. Kalaignar calls it folly beyond words. The Kural's irony is economic: wealth, the subject of Porutpaal, is spent to buy unawareness. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From anger, delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost, one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces how a clouded mind loses memory and then understanding.
hinduism.tie_back: The drinker in the Kural pays for the same sequence of delusion, lost self-awareness and downfall.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim, but the Gita is speaking about anger, not drink.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh: For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that heavy drinking leads to stupor and poverty.
christianity.tie_back: The bad bargain is the same: money goes out, and stupor and ruin come back.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified; close on the economic folly and the drowsy stupor.

islam.quote_or_event: “They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, ‘In them is great sin and [yet, some] benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an weighs wine's small gain against its far greater harm.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it judges drinking a losing bargain.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified; a cost-benefit framing close to the Kural's, without the self-oblivion image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas said: morning sleep, midday wine, children's talk and sitting in the assemblies of the ignorant put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: Wine in the middle of the day is listed among the habits that waste a person's life.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, drinking is something a person chooses that takes him out of his own life and purpose.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified; it shares the self-wasting idea but not the buying image.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The fifth lay precept is to refrain from surā-meraya-majja, intoxicants that are a ground for pamāda, heedlessness.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist ethics defines intoxicants by what they do: they produce heedlessness.
buddhism.tie_back: Pamāda is the Kural's meyyariyaamai, not knowing oneself.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Standard formula paraphrased; strong conceptual match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe gives Odysseus' men a mixture with Pramnian wine laced with drugs; they forget their homeland and are turned into swine.
greek_mythology.explanation: The men eagerly take a drink that robs them of memory and of their human selves.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They take a drink and receive self-forgetting in return, the Kural's meyyariyaamai.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Story summary; the potion is a drug, and the men do not pay for it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “penalties are doubled in the case of drunkenness; for the moving principle is in the man himself, since he had the power of not getting drunk and his getting drunk was the cause of his ignorance.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that ignorance a person brings on himself through drink does not excuse him; it makes him more blameworthy.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's argument exactly: whoever pays for his own ignorance chose his folly.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.5 (W. D. Ross trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified on the MIT Classics Archive; a precise conceptual match.

kurals.tamil:
துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
நஞ்சுண்பார் கள்ளுண் பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thunjinaar seththaarin verallar enjnjaandrum
nanjunpaar kallun pavar.
kurals.meaning: Just as sleepers are no different from the dead, those who drink liquor are always no different from people who swallow poison.
kurals.elementary: When someone is fast asleep, they can't see, hear or help anyone, almost as if they weren't there at all. The Kural says drinking liquor is like taking a little poison: it switches off your mind the same way.
kurals.university: The couplet is an udhaaranam (உதாரணம், exemplum) built on two equations. Thunjinaar (துஞ்சினார், those asleep) are 'not different from' (verallar, வேறல்லர்) seththaar (செத்தார், the dead), because both lack awareness. Likewise kallunbavar (கள்ளுண்பவர், toddy-drinkers) are always nanjunbaar (நஞ்சுண்பார், poison-eaters). Mu. Varadarasanar gives the shared term as arivu mayangudhal (அறிவு மயங்குதல், clouding of understanding). Puliyur Kesikan applies enjnjaandrum (எஞ்ஞான்றும், 'always') to the second clause: the drinker is permanently poisoned, while the sleeper only appears dead for a while. Kalaignar reverses the order and reads it as a hyperbole. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “What Kshatriya is there who, armed with weapons, will slay men locked in the embraces of sleep and, therefore, already dead?”
hinduism.explanation: At the drunken revel before the Yadavas' self-destruction, Satyaki taunts Kritavarma for killing sleeping warriors, men he calls ‘already dead’.
hinduism.tie_back: The epic uses the Kural's own equation of the sleeper with the dead, spoken in a scene where drink is the poison.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, Section 3 (K. M. Ganguli trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the sleep-equals-death image matches, though the speaker is not making the Kural's moral point.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober. For they that sleep sleep in the night; and they that be drunken are drunken in the night.”
christianity.explanation: Paul puts sleep and drunkenness side by side as two kinds of unawareness that belong to the night.
christianity.tie_back: This is the same pairing the Kural makes: the sleeper and the drinker are both absent from life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified; the sleep–drunkenness pairing is very close.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allāh and from prayer. So will you not desist?”
islam.explanation: Intoxicants cut a person off from remembering God and from prayer.
islam.tie_back: The drinker is spiritually ‘asleep’, as the Kural's drinker is as good as poisoned.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified; the harm it names is spiritual, with no poison or sleep image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They taught that an intoxicated person is responsible for all his actions only in a case where he did not reach the state of intoxication of Lot; however, if he reached the state of intoxication of Lot, so that he is altogether unaware of his actions, he is exempt from all liability.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud describes a level of drunkenness so deep that a person counts as no longer present as a moral agent.
judaism.tie_back: Lot's state is the Kural's sleeper-as-dead: there, but not aware.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 65a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified; a legal ruling rather than a warning, but the state it describes matches.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that heedfulness is the path to the Deathless and heedlessness the path to death; the heedful do not die, while the heedless are as if dead already.
buddhism.explanation: Heedlessness (pamāda), which intoxicants produce, is treated as a living death.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that losing awareness is already a kind of dying.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; the link to drink runs through the fifth precept.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Elpenor, youngest of Odysseus' crew, gets drunk at Circe's house, sleeps on the roof, and on waking falls and breaks his neck; his shade later meets Odysseus in the underworld.
greek_mythology.explanation: A drunken sleep becomes real death.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's chain of sleep, death and drink-as-poison happens literally to Elpenor.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Story summary; a striking literal match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For if you try to prove that the wise man can souse himself with much wine and yet keep his course straight, … you may go on to infer by syllogisms that he will not die if he swallows poison, that he will not sleep if he takes a sleeping-potion, …”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca mocks the idea that the wise can drink heavily unharmed, placing wine beside poison and sleeping draughts.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca puts wine, poison and sleep together just as the Kural does.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 83.27 (Gummere trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified on Wikisource; a remarkably close cluster of images.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளொற்றி உள்ளூர் நகப்படுவர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
கள்ளொற்றிக் கண்சாய் பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ullotri ulloor nagappaduvar enjnjaandrum
kallotrik kansaai pavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who drink in secret until their eyes droop will have their secret found out by their own townspeople, who will always laugh at them.
kurals.elementary: If you sneak cookies before dinner, the crumbs on your shirt give you away. The Kural says people who drink in secret are the same: their sleepy, drooping eyes tell everyone, and the whole neighbourhood ends up laughing.
kurals.university: The verb otri (ஒற்றி, 'in hiding') is used twice. Kal otri (கள்ளொற்றி) is drinking toddy secretly, and ul otri (உள்ளொற்றி) is the townsfolk spying out what is inside. Kansaaibavar (கண்சாய்பவர்) are 'those whose eyes droop', the physical sign that betrays them. Ulloor (உள்ளூர், one's own town) makes the mockery (nagappaduvar, நகப்படுவர், 'will be laughed at') come from neighbours, not strangers. Mu. Varadarasanar reads ul otri as the townsfolk probing into hidden matters. Kalaignar stresses that the reeling eyes cannot be hidden. thirukkural.net prints the couplet without the closing full stop; the wording is otherwise identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Manusmriti prescribes that a twice-born man convicted of drinking sura be branded on the forehead with the sign of a tavern flag, so that his offence is publicly visible and he is shunned.
hinduism.explanation: Drinking is made permanently public, so everyone in the community knows.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the drinker's secret ends in public exposure and scorn.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti, Chapter 9 (punishments for the great sins) (Bühler trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase without a verified verse number; a harsh legal parallel to social ridicule.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they also have erred through wine, and through strong drink are out of the way; the priest and the prophet have erred through strong drink, they are swallowed up of wine, … they err in vision, they stumble in judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Isaiah publicly exposes priests and prophets whose drinking shows in their failing sight and judgment.
christianity.tie_back: Even respected men cannot hide drink; it shows in the eyes and steps, as the Kural says.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified; public exposure is present, but secrecy and mockery are not.

islam.quote_or_event: When a man who had drunk wine was brought to the Prophet and beaten as a penalty, some onlookers cursed him; the Prophet forbade them, saying not to help Satan against their brother.
islam.explanation: The drinker's exposure brings the community's scorn, which the Prophet himself checks.
islam.tie_back: The townsfolk's ridicule the Kural describes is real, though Islam here restrains it with mercy.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Hudud (the drinker brought for punishment)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory without a verified hadith number; it adds a counterpoint of mercy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who cries, ‘Woe!’ who, ‘Alas!’; Who has quarrels, who complaints; Who has wounds without cause; Who has bleary eyes? Those whom wine keeps till the small hours, Those who gather to drain the cups.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs names the drinker's tell-tale bleary eyes, earned in late-night drinking.
judaism.tie_back: The ‘bleary eyes’ are the Kural's kansaai, drooping eyes that give the secret away.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified; very close on the eyes as evidence, with mockery implied.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The monk Sāgata, famed for taming a fierce nāga, was given strong drink by admiring lay followers and was found lying drunk at the town gate; the Buddha rebuked him before the Sangha and laid down the rule against intoxicants.
buddhism.explanation: A celebrated monk is exposed in public, and his fall brings the whole order into disrepute.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, drink exposed at the town gate turns respect into public shame.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Story summary from the Vinaya, not verified verbatim this session; a strong match on public exposure.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phrygian peasants find old Silenus wandering drunk, bind him with garlands and lead him to King Midas.
greek_mythology.explanation: Dionysus' companion is caught in drink and paraded before a king.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The drunk who stumbles is found out and made a spectacle by the locals, as in the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose parallel; Silenus is treated with honour, not mockery.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Besides, we forget who we are, we utter words that are halting and poorly enunciated, the glance is unsteady, the step falters, the head is dizzy, …”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca lists the bodily signs that give drunkenness away.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘The glance is unsteady’ is the Kural's kansaai: the eyes betray the hidden drinker.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 83.21 (Gummere trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified; matches the visible signs, but not the townsfolk's laughter.

kurals.tamil:
களித்தறியேன் என்பது கைவிடுக நெஞ்சத்து
ஒளித்ததூஉம் ஆங்கே மிகும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaliththariyen enbadhu kaividuka nenjaththu
oliththadhooum aange migum.
kurals.meaning: Let the drinker stop claiming ‘I have never been drunk’, because the moment he drinks, whatever he has hidden in his heart comes out even more.
kurals.elementary: It's like a shaken bottle of fizzy drink: open it and everything inside comes spraying out. The Kural says drink opens people up the same way, so pretending you never drink doesn't work. Your secrets fizz out the moment you do.
kurals.university: Kaliththariyen (களித்தறியேன்) is the drinker's own denial: 'I have never known intoxication.' Kaividuka (கைவிடுக, 'give it up') tells him to drop the lie. The reason is nenjaththu oliththadhooum (நெஞ்சத்து ஒளித்ததூஉம், 'even what was hidden in the heart'; the -ooum is an alapedai of -um, 'even') aange migum (ஆங்கே மிகும், 'there and then increases', that is, comes out all the more). Mu. Varadarasanar reads the hidden thing as the hidden fault; Puliyur Kesikan as the earlier concealment of drinking itself; Kalaignar as the truth that the drunk man blurts out. The idea is close to the Graeco-Roman proverb 'in wine, truth'. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the Prabhasa revel the drunken Yadava heroes bring up old, buried grievances: Satyaki's contempt for Kritavarma's night massacre, Kritavarma's taunt about Bhurishrava, and the affair of the Syamantaka gem. The quarrel turns into slaughter.
hinduism.explanation: Resentments hidden for years come out the moment wine loosens the heroes' tongues.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's warning in narrative form: drink brings out what was hidden in the heart.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, Section 3 (K. M. Ganguli trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Summary of a text verified this session; a strong narrative match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that under wine the heart speaks out its distortions.
christianity.tie_back: The ‘heart’ that ‘utters’ is the Kural's nenjaththu oliththadhu, what is hidden in the heart, coming out.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified; close on the heart revealing itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “Avoid Khamr for it is the mother of all evils. … He said: ‘Pour me a cup of this wine.’ So she poured him a cup. He said: ‘Give me more.’ And soon he had intercourse with her and killed the boy.”
islam.explanation: Uthman tells of a devout worshipper who chose wine as the ‘least’ of three sins, and drink then led him into the other two.
islam.tie_back: The cup lets out every evil the man had held back, as the Kural warns.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on sunnah.com; about drink unleashing sin rather than revealing secrets.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wine [yayin] was given in seventy letters, … Similarly, the word secret [sod] was given in seventy letters, … Typically, when wine entered the body, a secret emerged.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud notes that 'wine' and 'secret' have the same numerical value of seventy: when wine goes in, the secret comes out.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost word for word the Kural's claim that drink brings out what the heart hid.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 65a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one's own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another's faults, but hides one's own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada describes the habit of hiding one's own faults.
buddhism.tie_back: The drinker who denies drinking is hiding his fault, which the Kural says cannot stay hidden.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified; about hiding faults in general, not about drink.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The lyric poet Alcaeus is credited with the saying that wine and truth go together, the origin of the Latin proverb in vino veritas.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tradition held that wine strips away pretence and lets the truth out.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: whatever is hidden comes out with wine.
greek_mythology.source: Alcaeus, fragment (via the proverb ‘in vino veritas’)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Attribution through secondary tradition; Greek lyric, not myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “When the strength of wine has become too great and has gained control over the mind, every lurking evil comes forth from its hiding-place. Drunkenness does not create vice, it merely brings it into view; …”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca says drink does not create vices but exposes those already present.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's nenjaththu oliththadhooum aange migum almost exactly.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 83.20 (Gummere trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified on Wikisource; a near one-to-one match.

kurals.tamil:
களித்தானைக் காரணம் காட்டுதல் கீழ்நீர்க்
குளித்தானைத் தீத்துரீஇ அற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaliththaanaik kaaranam kaattudhal keezhneerk
kuliththaanaith theeththureei atru.
kurals.meaning: Trying to reason with a drunk man is like searching with a burning torch for someone who has sunk deep under water.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your friend has dived to the bottom of a pool and you try to find him by shining a candle from the side. The water puts the flame out and you can't reach him. The Kural says giving good reasons to someone who is drunk is like that: your words can't get through.
kurals.university: Kaaranam kaattudhal (காரணம் காட்டுதல், 'showing reasons') is set against keezhneer kuliththaan (கீழ்நீர்க் குளித்தான், 'one who has plunged into deep water'), and the attempt is theeththureei atru (தீத்துரீஇ அற்று, 'like searching with fire'). Thuru (துருவுதல்) means to probe or search, and the -eei is an alapedai lengthening. The image works twice over: fire cannot burn under water, and a drowned man is beyond help. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as trying to sober or reform the drinker with arguments. Puliyur Kesikan takes kaaranam kaattudhal as pointing to another drunk as a warning, which leads into Kural 930. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Kishkindha Kanda, Sugriva, restored to his throne, sinks into drink and pleasure and forgets his promise to Rama; earlier counsel has no effect, and only Lakshmana's furious arrival at the gates rouses him.
hinduism.explanation: Reasoning cannot reach a king lost in revelry; only a shock brings him back.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural says, reasons do not reach someone sunk in drink.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Summary from memory, not verified this session; the emphasis on drink varies between retellings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoredom and wine and new wine take away the heart.”
christianity.explanation: Hosea says wine takes away the ‘heart’, which in Hebrew thought is the seat of understanding.
christianity.tie_back: Once understanding is gone, there is nothing left for reasons to work on, which is why the Kural's torch is useless.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified; explains why reasoning fails, without the image.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying …”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an recognises that an intoxicated person does not know what he is saying, so prayer has to wait until he is sober.
islam.tie_back: If the drinker cannot follow his own words, others' reasons will not reach him either, as the Kural says.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified; the shared point is that the drunk mind cannot be reached.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You will be like one lying in bed on high seas, Like one lying on top of the rigging. ‘They struck me, but I felt no hurt; They beat me, but I was unaware; …’”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs pictures the drunkard as someone lost at sea who feels nothing.
judaism.tie_back: The sea image matches the Kural's man under water whom no light or reason can reach.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified; a close match on both the water image and the unreachable mind.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who is drunk, poor, destitute, still thirsty whilst drinking, frequents the bars, sinks in debt as a stone in water, swiftly brings disrepute to his family.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the drinker sinking ‘as a stone in water’, still thirsty even while drinking.
buddhism.tie_back: The sinking stone matches the Kural's drowned man, beyond reach.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified; the water image matches, but the futility of reasoning is not stated.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the wedding of Pirithous, the drunken centaurs led by Eurytus try to carry off the bride; no appeal stops them, and the feast becomes the battle of the Lapiths and Centaurs.
greek_mythology.explanation: Once the centaurs are drunk, only force can stop them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As the Kural says, reasoning is useless against the drunk.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose thematic parallel; the story does not show anyone trying to reason with them.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that people in a state like drunkenness can repeat proofs or recite verses of Empedocles without their knowledge actually working, like those asleep, mad or drunk.
philosophy.explanation: The drunk may hear words, even repeat them, but the reasoning does not engage.
philosophy.tie_back: The torch is lit, but it cannot work under water.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VII.3 (W. D. Ross trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not verified this session; a good conceptual match.

kurals.tamil:
கள்ளுண்ணாப் போழ்திற் களித்தானைக் காணுங்கால்
உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kallunnaap pozhdhir kaliththaanaik kaanungaal
ullaankol undadhan sorvu.
kurals.meaning: When a drinker is sober and sees someone else reeling drunk, does he not think that he looks the same when he drinks?
kurals.elementary: Have you ever laughed at someone acting silly, then realised you act just like that sometimes? The Kural asks why a drinker, seeing another person drunk and stumbling, doesn't think, ‘Oh no, that's me when I drink!’
kurals.university: The closing couplet is a rhetorical question marked by kol (கொல்). When the drinker, in kallunnaap pozhdhu (கள்ளுண்ணாப் போழ்து, 'the time he is not drinking'), sees a kaliththaan (களித்தான், a drunk man), will he not reflect, ullaan (உள்ளான், 'will he not consider'), on the sorvu (சோர்வு, slackness, lapse) that comes from his own drinking? The appeal is to self-recognition. Commentators agree on this reading: Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesikan all take it as a sober drinker seeing his own condition in another. Mu. Varadarasanar's printed gloss reads மயங்கினவளை ('the intoxicated woman') on both base sites, apparently a typographical slip for மயங்கினவனை. The text is identical on ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The learned Sukra, having been deceived while under the influence of wine, and remembering the total loss of consciousness that is one of the terrible consequences of drink, and beholding too before him the handsome Kacha whom he had, in a state of unconsciousness, drunk with his wine, then thought of effecting a reform in the manners of Brahmanas.”
hinduism.explanation: Once sober, Shukra looks back at what drink made him do and acts on it.
hinduism.tie_back: Shukra does what the Kural hopes every sober drinker will do: reflect and change.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 76 (K. M. Ganguli trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified; Shukra reflects on his own lapse rather than on another drunk.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus calls on his hearers to watch themselves so that drunkenness does not catch them unprepared.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Take heed to yourselves’ is the same self-examination the Kural asks of the sober drinker.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified; it shares the call to self-watchfulness but has no image of seeing another drunk.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allāh and from prayer. So will you not desist?”
islam.explanation: After setting out the harms of intoxicants, the Qur'an ends with a pointed question.
islam.tie_back: ‘So will you not desist?’ has the same rhetorical form as the Kural's ‘will he not reflect?’
islam._accuracy_note: Verified; strong match in rhetorical form, and the appeal to reflection is shared.

judaism.quote_or_event: “‘They struck me, but I felt no hurt; They beat me, but I was unaware; As often as I wake, I go after it again.’”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs gives the drinker's own voice: he wakes, feels nothing, and goes straight back to the cup.
judaism.tie_back: This is the failure the Kural laments: the drinker who, even when sober, will not reflect.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified; a close match on the failure to reflect.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kumbha Jataka, Sakka appears before King Sabbamitta carrying a jar of liquor and describes in verse everything the drink will do to him; the king, seeing the effects laid out before he drinks, gives up liquor.
buddhism.explanation: A vivid picture of drunkenness's effects leads a king to renounce it while still sober.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the reflection the Kural hopes for: seeing the effects and applying them to oneself.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Story summary from memory, not verified this session; a good thematic match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the wine must have been doing you a mischief, as it does with all those drink immoderately. It was wine that inflamed the Centaur Eurytion …”
greek_mythology.explanation: The suitor Antinous lectures the disguised Odysseus on the ruin wine brings, while drinking heavily himself; in the next book he is shot down with the cup at his lips.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Antinous sees drink's folly in others but never in himself, the blindness the Kural asks about.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified (Book 21); a close dramatic irony matching the Kural's question.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch reports that the Spartans would make helots drink unmixed wine and bring them into the common messes, to show the young men what drunkenness looked like.
philosophy.explanation: Spartan education used the sight of a drunk man to teach sobriety.
philosophy.tie_back: This puts into practice the Kural's hope that seeing another drunk will make a person reflect.
